author: Omar Kalinge-Nnyago
title: Uganda: The Entrenchment of a Hereditary Military Oligarchy
content:
Uganda is approaching one of the most precarious political transitions in its post-independence history. The likely trajectory is not democratic consolidation but the slow institutionalization of a hereditary military oligarchy. Four developments are driving this shift: President Yoweri Museveni’s advanced age; the elevation of his son, Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, to Chief of Defence Forces (CDF); the operationalization of the Patriotic League of Uganda (PLU) as a parallel mobilization vehicle; and the legal entrenchment of military authority over civilian institutions. Taken together, these amount to what might be called a “slow-motion coup” already under way.


The most probable outcome is best described as contested dynastic authoritarianism, a system in which elections continue to serve as instruments of international legitimacy, while substantive power is contested within the first family and the military elite rather than at the ballot box. The formal opposition faces structural decapitation through repression and co-optation. Yet two under-examined institutions – the Anglican and Catholic Churches, and segments of Uganda’s Muslim community – offer potential, if imperfect, nonviolent pathways for mediation or resistance over the coming decade, complicated by the risk of Muslim youth radicalization.


A conventional, extra-constitutional military coup remains possible even as the regime works to secure de facto military dominance through promotions, strategic retirements of senior officers, legislative amendment, and patronage. The PLU’s grassroots strategy is designed to insulate the succession from exactly this risk, cultivating broad loyalty and framing dynastic continuity as patriotic inevitability rather than rupture. The principal danger to the plan, accordingly, lies less in popular revolt than in intra-elite fracture or palace intrigue should the succession falter.


Anatomy of a slow-motion coup


The regime has moved beyond personalist autocracy toward a durable, self-perpetuating system built on four pillars: fusion of military command with the first family, political mobilization through the PLU, subordination of parliament, and kleptocratic control of the state’s resources.


Uganda’s slide toward dynastic rule no longer needs to be projected; it can be observed directly. In 2024, Museveni handed his son the office of Chief of Defence Forces, together with an unusual personal grant of authority to promote senior officers – a clear departure from the constitutional design of a professional military answerable to civilian rather than familial command. Muhoozi has used this platform expansively, maintaining an active, often combative social media presence, intervening openly in partisan disputes, and, in June 2026, ordering troops to shut down Nation Media Group’s operations after critical coverage of his conduct. He has also directly ordered the arrest of opposition lawyer Erias Lukwago and the deportation of Kenyan lawyer Martha Karua, both members of Dr Kizza Besigye’s defence team – a signal that the regime now treats defence counsel, and not only defendants, as targets. In his national address of 4 July 2026, President Museveni appeared to defend his son’s actions, placing blame on Besigye for allegedly delaying court proceedings.


The institutional scaffolding around Muhoozi has matured alongside his personal profile. The Patriotic League of Uganda, rebranded in 2024 from an informal network of birthday rallies and fan clubs known as the “Muhoozi Project”, now runs village-level structures, community clean-up campaigns, and youth roadshows, and openly courts the same rural base the National Resistance Movement (NRM) has cultivated for four decades. It functions less as a political party than as an insurance policy: it absorbs potential rivals into patronage, builds a loyalty network running parallel to the NRM’s own, and softens the ground for a hereditary handover by presenting it as continuity rather than rupture. Leadership changes, such as the appointment of Hon. Fadil Twaha as Secretary General, signal a deliberate effort to deepen outreach among Muslim communities that feel marginalized in the League’s rise.


The 12

th

 Parliament offered an early demonstration of the PLU’s reach. The League withdrew its earlier backing for then Speaker Anita Among and her deputy, Thomas Tayebwa, clearing the way for Jacob Oboth-Oboth’s election as Speaker – a small but telling exercise of veto power …

title: Morocco’s First Woman Prime Minister and the Terms of Freedom
content:
Something changes when a woman occupies an office men have treated as their natural inheritance. Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri’s

appointment

 on 29 September 2026 makes that change visible in Morocco. For women whose competence is routinely scrutinised, the pleasure is neither naïve nor trivial.


But the woman forming a government and the woman labouring in the fields, raising children without pay and denied an equal share of her inheritance encounter power differently. Representation changes who governs; emancipation changes what all women have the power to do. That distinction shifts our attention from PM Mansouri’s gender to the politics of the centre-right

 Party of Authenticity and Modernity (PAM

)

, which she leads. Will its programme redistribute the resources and rights on which women’s freedom depends?


The history beneath the headline


Calling women’s leadership foreign to Morocco requires forgetting its history. Historian Osire Glacier

documents

 women’s authority long before the contemporary premiership. Kenza al Awrabiya, the Amazigh mother of Idris II, helped secure the Idrisid dynasty, founded in the late eighth century in what is now Morocco. Zaynab al Nafzawiyya influenced eleventh-century Almoravid politics around Aghmat, near Marrakech. Sayyida al Hurra governed Tétouan, a city in northern Morocco, during the sixteenth century. Khnata bint Bakkar intervened in eighteenth-century dynastic politics.


Across the region,

Dihya

 is remembered as an Amazigh queen who led resistance to the Arab conquest in the Aurès, in present-day Algeria, during the late seventh century. Tuareg oral tradition remembers

Tin Hinan

 as a queen and founding ancestress of noble lineages in the Ahaggar, in present-day southern Algeria.


These histories expose how male authority is made to appear natural. Fatima Mernissi’s

The Forgotten Queens of Islam


challenges that selective memory. Colonialism also reorganised authority: French Protectorate administrators

reshaped

 customary courts around imperial priorities. What survives as tradition can carry the history of political intervention. 


Religious interpretation can give exclusion another claim to permanence. Islamist and other conservative opponents invoke this

hadith

 against women’s political authority:


«لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ وَلَّوْا أَمْرَهُمُ امْرَأَةً»


Usually translated as saying that a people governed by a woman will not prosper, it becomes a prohibition irrespective of her competence. Asma Lamrabet, a

Moroccan Islamic feminist thinker

, questions turning a

narration linked

 to Persia’s dynastic succession into a universal ban. She reads it against the Qur’anic Queen of Sheba, whose judgement demonstrates capable leadership. Her argument contests male authority’s claim to divine necessity.


PAM’s promises and its record


Women have long contested how authority is distributed within the family. Fatima Sadiqi

documents

the Union de l’Action Féminine’s 1992 million-signature campaign to reform the Moudawana, Morocco’s family code. The 2004 reform abolished wives’ duty of obedience but retained unequal inheritance and exceptions to the marriage age of eighteen. Proposals announced in December 2024 left fundamental equality demands unresolved. In October 2025, more than sixty civil society organisations and public figures

joined to call for comprehensive reform

. Rights in Morocco have advanced through organised demands, not the gender of an officeholder.


PAM, a centre-right party founded in 2008,

advocates

 social modernisation and positions itself against the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD). It entered government in 2021 alongside the National Rally of Independents and conservative nationalist Istiqlal. Opposition to Islamist conservatism, however, does not itself entail reforming the laws and economic conditions that subordinate women.


PAM’s

2026 programme

 promises improved widow pensions, childcare, safe transport, a women’s enterprise fund and labour inspection. The commitments leave inheritance equality, abortion reform and decriminalisation of consensual same sex relations unaddressed. Mansouri called for

banning child marriage

 without exceptions in 2024, yet PAM’s electoral programme

omits that commitment

. Employment can support independence, but a wage does not cancel criminalisation or unequal property rights. The programme leaves those constraints intact.


Even PAM’s narrow promise to increase …

author: WoMin
title: Press Release | Women’s Climate Assembly strengthens Pan African solidarity, women-led resistance and the struggle for a just future
content:
“

Empowering women is a radical way to transform the world!

” –

Ivorian activist


The fourth regional

Women’s Climate Assembly

 (WCA), held in Yaoundé, Cameroon, from 5–8 October 2026, concluded with a powerful reaffirmation of African women’s determination to defend their lands, territories, livelihoods and communities, and to demand climate justice and reparations.


Under the theme, “

Our lands, our voices: African women united for climate justice and reparations!

”, the Assembly convened over 75 women community leaders, activists, feminist organisations, civil society groups and allies from twelve countries including Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Guinea-Conakry, Liberia, Namibia, Niger, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Senegal and Zambia.


The gathering provided a vital space for women on the frontlines of the climate crisis, extractive industries, land dispossession and environmental destruction to share their experiences, strengthen relationships across borders and build collective strategies for change.


As the Assembly closed, one message rang clear: African women are not merely bearing the costs of the climate crisis. They are leading the struggle for solutions, defending their communities and shaping the future they want.


“

There’s an adage in my village that women cannot build a nation. The Women’s Climate Assembly has proved that women build nations. We counter this adage with the unity and solidarity of African women!”

 –

DRC activist-participant


Turning shared struggles into collective power


From communities confronting oil and gas expansion and destructive mining to women defending forests, seeds, water sources and ancestral lands, participants brought forward the lived realities of communities too often excluded from decisions about their territories and futures.


Through collective reflection, popular education and movement-building, women connected struggles that may take place in different countries but are rooted in common systems of exploitation, inequality and environmental destruction.


Designed by women activists and members of the WCA Steering Committee, the thematic teach-ins explored a range of political concepts, questions and practices, including:


The erosion of farmers’ seeds

: A challenge for building resilient and sustainable food systems. What solutions are there for preserving our seed heritage?  


Nature Commons

: The defence of the Congo Basin’s forests.


Counting the Costs of Mal/Bad Development and Demanding reparations

: The case of the African Development Bank campaign.


Fighting some of the false solutions to the climate crisis

: Gas extraction, enclosure of our forests and lands for carbon trading, green conservation and more.


Building democratic, accountable, ‘loving’ leadership

: Why are these principles so important to feminist leadership? What else do we feel is critical to leading as feminists?


Lessons on organising and movement building

: Growing National/sub-regional grassroots movements.


Building knowledge from what we know

: Building feminist popular knowledge as the basis for Building Women’s Power. How can we go about doing this locally in our communities and beyond that.


The WCA celebrated the knowledge, resistance and organising power of rural, Indigenous, peasant and working-class women. The

Each One, Teach One

 sessions embodied this spirit of knowledge-sharing, collective learning and liberation. On Day Two, participants exchanged practical skills, crafts and tools, sharing techniques for making baobab candies, producing eco-briquettes from cassava and creating seed bricks to cultivate and protect Indigenous seeds. Weaving, cloth-dyeing, beadwork and other practices also featured, affirming the value of knowledge held, practised and passed down through generations of women.


The gathering reaffirmed the importance of strengthening a Pan African ecofeminist movement that recognises the connections between the climate crisis, extractivism, gender injustice, food insecurity and the loss of community control over natural resources.


It also reinforced a fundamental principle: communities must have the power to determine their own futures, including the right to say NO to destructive development projects that threaten their lands, livelihoods and ways of life.


Climate justice means reparations, not empty promises

author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: Mada Masr
title: Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah referred to trial on charges of running unlicensed website
content:
Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah was referred to trial on Thursday on charges of establishing and managing a website without a license, according to lawyer Hassan al-Azhari, Mada Masr’s legal counsel.


The Supreme State Security Prosecution referred Attalah to trial at a New Cairo misdemeanors court, where sessions will begin on October 27.


The referral decision came after Attallah was questioned for over six hours by prosecutors on Wednesday at the Supreme State Security Prosecution headquarters in New Cairo. Prosecutors questioned her during the session on charges of running a website without a license and of publishing false news with the aim of disturbing public peace, with the latter accusation dropped from the charge sheet in the trial referral.


Azhari described the “haste” in the trial referral, which came just hours after the interrogation closed, and its scheduling for the coming week as “unjustified urgency” given the absence of circumstances in the case that require rapid resolution.


Wednesday’s investigation, labelled Supreme State Security Prosecution Case 9072/26, comprised information and documents compiled by the National Security Agency, including a report Mada Masr published earlier this month describing a

wave of protests in prisons after the postponement of the criminal procedures law

, as well as a letter from the Supreme Media Regulatory Council regarding the legal status of website’s license, Azhari said.

 


The latest application for a license has been pending without response since 2023, after Mada Masr submitted additional supporting materials to the media council for consideration, according to Azhari.


Mada Masr has applied on multiple occasions for a license to operate since 2018, when a new law was passed organizing the media and the press, and again in 2020, upon the issuance of the bylaws.


It received no response from the council, and was informed instead by prosecutors, during a separate interrogation in which Attalah was

summoned

 in 2022, that the SMRC had rejected its license application. 


A  lawsuit was filed by the website in 2022

challenging

 the SMRC’s decision and its failure to inform the organization of its rejection. During a session in the case in 2023, Mada Masr received for the first time information on the SMRC’s basis for rejecting its request, which included that a number of the required documents were not included. 


According to Azhari, the prescribed penalty for the charges facing Attalah is a fine of not less than LE1 million and not exceeding LE3  million.

As per Article 105 of the press and media regulation l

aw

, the court may also order the closure and confiscation of equipment and devices used in committing the “crime,” and the doubling of the fine in case of recurrence.

The post

Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah referred to trial on charges of running unlicensed website

 first appeared on

Mada Masr

author: Fraser Needham
title: NDP MP says only most extreme forms of residential school denialism should be considered hate crimes
content:
A Winnipeg NDP MP says the party has no intention of limiting free speech and wants to see residential school denialism made a prosecutable hate crime in only the most extreme circumstances.


“We’re not talking about dinner conversations,” said

Lean Gazan

 [Winnipeg Centre] a member of the Wood Mountain Lakota Nation. “We’re not talking about someone sharing an opinion or trying to learn. I’m talking about folks that have participated in the mass spreading of disinformation.


“Folks like Tom Flanagan who wrote Grave Hoax (Grave Error: How The Media Misled Us (and the Truth about Residential Schools). Folks that have gone to T’kemlups Te Secwepemc territory that were protesting resulting from that disinformation.”


Toronto Metropolitan University professor Pam Palmater, who is a member of the Mi’kmaq Nation, also says there are grounds and precedent for making residential school denialism a hate crime in certain cases.


“The Holocaust, which was horrific, that happened in another country has been made a hate crime here in terms of denial of it,” she said. “So, we have a precedent for denying things like the Holocaust which is a form of genocide. Well we’ve had a national inquiry that confirmed Canada has been guilty of genocide. Given that the Indian residential schools was one of the key aspects of those genocidal laws, policies and practices – why on earth wouldn’t we criminalize it’s denialism here in this country.”


Some First Nations politicians, such as Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew and Conservative MP Billy Morin have argued residential school denialism shouldn’t be considered a hate crime.


Bill C-254

 has had one reading in the House of Commons.


Revenues from major projects


A new draft paper by the Assembly of First Nations argues all First Nations should benefit from revenues produced by major projects of national economic interest and not just those whose lands are directly affected.


“Basically what they (AFN) propose in this draft is they want to create a fund that owns that 10 per cent equity in that oil pipeline (Pacific Link) on behalf of First Nations, controlled by First Nations, and they would like to disperse the payments and the equity across Canada for all First Nations so that way it’s more equal, it’s more fair and no First Nations get left out ,” APTN News Ottawa web reporter Keelan Jacobs said.


The proposal is included in a draft paper put together for by the AFN for an upcoming meeting between First Nations, Prime Minister Mark Carney and provincial and territorial premiers slated to take place in Ottawa on Monday.


The AFN is a political organization that represents more than 600 First Nations.


The government has offered First Nations a minimum 10 per cent investment in the proposed Pacific Link pipeline which would transport oil from Alberta to British Columbia’s west coast for transport to foreign markets.


APTN News obtained a

copy of the AFN’s draft proposal last week.


The post

NDP MP says only most extreme forms of residential school denialism should be considered hate crimes

 appeared first on

APTN News

.

author: Daron Letts
title: Nunavut MLAs reconvene for fall sitting
content:
Members of Nunavut’s seventh legislative assembly convened in Iqaluit Thursday afternoon, following their four-month summer break.


Speaker David Joanasie opened with words of solace for the families of the four soldiers killed and 39 injured in Saturday’s fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, in Alberta.

Flags have flown at half mast at government buildings all week.


Premier John Main also referred to Albertans in his opening statement, praising the result of Monday’s provincial referendum, in which 75 per cent of voters rejected holding another referendum on separating from Canada.


“I was pleased to see a strong result reflecting a desire to remain in Canada,” Main said.


His sentiments were later echoed by Cambridge Bay MLA Fred Pedersen, who thanked Albertans.


“This alleviates a lot of fears and questions that Kitikmeot residents and this government would have faced if the result was different,”

Pedersen said.


Health Minister Janet Brewster announced the launch of p

ublic health’s fall immunization campaign, which includes influenza and COVID-19 vaccination clinics this fall for Nunavummiut aged six months and older. An enhanced flu vaccine is also available for those aged 65 and older, Brewster said.


Nurses vaccinated MLAs, government staff and visitors to the legislative assembly throughout much of the day.


“Receiving seasonal immunizations every fall helps protect our most vulnerable community members, including our elders,” Brewster said.


Members also welcomed their newest colleague, Jason Iqaluq of Sanikiluaq, who was elected to represent the Hudson Bay riding in a Sept. 28

byelection

.

He replaces Daniel Qavvik, who resigned from the legislature in June.


“The need for the community infrastructure remains great,” Iqaluq said in his opening address. “I will be working with local leadership to advocate for investment.”


The Legislative Assembly returns for the first reading of several bills on Friday morning. The sitting ends Nov. 5.

author: Chris Walker
title: Trump Critic Louise Lucas Indicted as DOJ Ignores Election-Year Guidelines
content:
“I spent my life fighting back, and I’m not stopping now,” said Virginia State Sen. Louise Lucas.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

On Thursday, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) announced a slew of charges against Virginia State Sen. Louise Lucas (D), a critic of President Donald Trump and a proponent of redistricting that was attempted earlier this year in response to overtly partisan GOP gerrymandering efforts elsewhere in the country.

The DOJ indictment includes charges of racketeering, money laundering, and unlawful marijuana distribution. Six individuals were charged along with Lucas, including some members of her family.

Lucas, the president pro tempore of the Virginia Senate, has denied the charges levied against her, claiming they were issued for political reasons.

“I grew up under Jim Crow. I’ve seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my life fighting back, and I’m not stopping now,” she said in a statement posted to X.

“I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down,” Lucas added.

Generally, to avoid the appearance of partisanship, the DOJ will not issue charges against politicians within a 60-day window of elections. However, Attorney General Todd Blanche dismissed those concerns, claiming that the Justice Department didn’t have to follow that standard.

“It’s not even a rule, it’s a practice,” Blanche said at the press briefing announcing the charges against Lucas.

In 2024, however, then-candidate for president Donald Trump disagreed. When charges against him were unsealed within a month of Election Day that year, Trump cited the rule as proof that the DOJ, under the Biden administration, was engaging in “election interference.” Blanche was Trump’s legal counsel at that time.

(Notably, the circumstances in that situation were much different, as the charges against Trump in the election subversion case were issued outside of the 60-day window, but delays due to appeals from his legal team resulted in their being unsealed much later.)

The indictment against Lucas comes just a week and a half after federal agents raided the Washington, D.C. residence of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minnesota), another vocal critic of the president and a frequent target of his rage-filled social media posts. This past week, border czar Tom Homan confirmed that the investigation into Omar stems from supposed questions relating to her initial application for U.S. citizenship, despite previous investigations into the matter yielding no evidence of wrongdoing by her when she applied as a minor. Homan said that the administration is looking into plans to “denaturalize” Omar.

In an interview on Wednesday, Omar indicated that she would not move back into the residence that was raided, saying that attention on her home has made her feel unsafe there. She added that she is “confident in the fact that I didn’t do anything wrong,” regarding her application to be a citizen over two decades ago.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Santana Dreaver
title: ‘Gratifying and humbling’: First Nation leads ghost net cleanup from Interior ‘B.C.’ rivers
content:
Volunteers Lyza Adoplh, John Redan, Nick Froese and Roxx Ledoux work to haul abandoned fishing gear out of the Fraser and Thompson rivers. Photo by Santana Dreaver


This article has been co-published

with the Narwhal

 as part of their

2026 Indigenous journalism fellowship

.


After starting the day with a prayer and a safety demonstration, a group of volunteers gears up in water-resistant clothing and lifejackets, ready to hit the water.


The crew is preparing to scour a stretch of the Fraser and Thompson rivers, removing any fishing gear or waste left behind. Fishing nets left underneath the water are commonly known as ghost nets, which trap and kill fish. 


As the saying goes on a volunteer call out poster, “ghost nets create ghost fish.”


TLKemchEEN (Lytton First Nation) has led the river clean-up program in the area for the past 20 years, all in an effort to preserve salmon populations and aquatic life following harvest season.


Over two days in September, a group of 40 volunteers spent a total of 20 combined hours on the water.


From Lillooet to Lytton during the first day, and from Lytton to Yale during the second day, volunteers passed through white-water rapids and rugged terrain such as the famously turbulent passage of Hell’s Gate.


When the raft leader yells “hold on,” that’s exactly what participants do, reaching down for a rope attached to the raft, laughing and hollering, ripping through the Fraser Canyon rapids. 


The cold river water splashes everyone — waking up the crew as countless bald and golden eagles watch from above.


“I didn’t realize how impactful everything is along the shores. I guess I didn’t realize that some leave their garbage and nets out there,” volunteer Rebecca Riley, who is from the Stʼatʼimc Nation, said.


“Once I saw that with my own eyes, I wanted to jump in and be a part of it.”


A newspaper ad about the river clean-up project inspired Rebecca Riley to get involved. She has helped remove ghost nets since 2018. Photo: Supplied by Rebecca Riley


‘That fishery is a communal right’


It’s a sentiment shared by many volunteers on the boat, who eagerly approach the shoreline when a ghost net comes into sight. 


Whether the net will take one person to remove, or up to five to pull out of the water, is unknown until people get their hands wet. 


During the non-rapid portion of the cleanup, countless stories were told, Indigenous people exchanged words in their languages to compare similarities and differences and folks even had hot chocolate along the shore, courtesy of Kumsheen Rafting, which was contracted to support the program this year. 


During the first year of the program, 126 ghost nets were collected.


“This year we picked up six nets and some garbage, some years prior we’ve picked up zero. We have to remind our fishermen not to be lazy and take their gear home,” Kevin Duncan told the Narwhal.


Duncan is an elected councillor for TLKemchEEN in “B.C.’s” Southern Interior, part of the Nlaka’pamux Nation Tribal Council. He has been involved with the program since its inception. He attended both cleanup days this year with his son, Aaron.


Kevin Duncan, an elected councillor for TLKemchEEN, has been involved in Lytton’s ghost net clean-up initiative since it started 20 years ago. He always leads a prayer before they begin. Photo: Supplied by Rebecca Riley


For TLKemchEEN, stewarding their waters as they always have is crucial — especially as salmon numbers decline. Life along the Fraser and Thompson rivers is deeply connected to salmon. And TLKemchEEn is home to where the two rivers meet, in the country’s largest salmon-bearing watershed.


“For future generations, sometime down the road, I’m afraid all they’re going to be looking at is pictures of salmon in a book,” said Duncan. 


The nets recovered by the program are given to those in need, including single mothers, low-income families and Elders from the nation. 


“As a Nlaka’pamux or Stʼatʼimc member … that fishery is a communal right, it’s not an individual right. It’s looked after by your nation,” Duncan said.


“Most times, you just get to see portions of the river from the highway, but once you’re down on the water, floating for eight hours from Lillooet to Lytton, it gives you a better perspective on where people fish.” 


Now 20 years into the program, volunteer spots fill up months in advance. Photo by Santana Dreaver


Removing fishing gear from the cold and fast-moving river can be …

author: C4SS
title: C4SS Panelists on the Enduring Legacy of Don Lavoie
content:
The

Markets and Society conference

 this weekend (October 23-26) will feature many interesting panels on topics from public policy to self-governance to digital privacy to immigration and beyond. There will also be longtime C4SSers presenting.


On

Saturday from 9:00-10:30am

, Nathan Goodman is chairing the panel “The Enduring Legacy of Don Lavoie” featuring:


Cory Massimino – National Economic Planning: What is Right?


Don Lavoie argued in “National Economic Planning: What is Left?” that economic planning was inherently reactionary and thwarted genuinely left-wing aims like peace and liberation. Despite the prevailing conservative-libertarian fusionism of Lavoie’s day, his study of economics and history helped him see the transience of such an alliance: libertarianism was left-wing until the left became obsessed with economic planning and the right was always about militarism and hierarchy no matter how much libertarian rhetoric it adopted. Lavoie’s new (yet old) framing went under appreciated during his time and deserves careful reconsidering for anticipating the contemporary right’s increasing authoritarianism. This essay will build on Lavoie’s framing of economic planning as essentially right-wing, apply that framing to the contemporary American political situation, and argue such a framing is essential for any coherent conception of the political landscape going forward.


Jason Lee Byas – A Role For Lavoian Democracy


Don Lavoie argues for detaching our concept of democracy from the particular institution of voting, and instead seeing it as “openness,” or accessible means to shaping the world around you and its rules. An advantage of this approach is its complementarity with markets and property rights, which might otherwise be seen as in tension with democracy — thus partially reuniting liberalism’s “libertarian” and “democratic” commitments. Yet there is still a tension here. Philosophically, many libertarians may think that any social rules involving force should simply be set by natural rights, and so leaving these open to adjustment by anyone at all (let alone with open access to everyone) will be a problem. Practically, open access to reshaping the rules may spell uncertainty in problematic ways. I resolve these remaining tensions by suggesting a specific role for Lavoian Democracy. In short, many things are left radically indeterminate by any socially-practiced system of rights, and so too are many things left radically indeterminate by a commitment to natural rights. Questions of interpretation and resolution loom large, and the process of interpretation and resolution can either be hierarchical and authoritarian, or a product of ground-up contestation. There are principled liberal grounds — both moral and epistemic — for favoring the latter, and this is the role for Lavoian Democracy. I then offer a handful of institutions and practices that Lavoian Democracy might favor, including unions (of a certain form), adverse possession, and the common law.


Akiva Malamet – Beyond Recognition: Identity, Cultural Discovery, and the Limits of Social Planning


Scholars in liberal theory and political economy have long emphasized what Don Lavoie called the “knowledge problem”: social information is dispersed, local, emergent, and personal, and thus inaccessible to centralized or “high modernist” institutions. Lavoie and others showed that state economic planning fails because planners cannot access or generate this kind of knowledge and often undermine its creation. Liberal institutions, by contrast, enable people to align diverse plans and generate forms of knowledge no top-down authority could anticipate. I extend these insights to issues of identity, cultural development, and interpersonal life. Identity and cultural formation are bottom-up, organic processes reflecting the nuances of how people self-conceive, relate, and find meaning. State planning and institutional treatments of identity often obstruct pluralistic self-concepts and cultural discovery, flattening human diversity and complex individual lives into simple, legible categories. Ironically, formal recognition can perpetuate the injustices it was intended to remedy and reinforce intergroup conflict. State recognition of identity undermines the processes through which identity becomes meaningful, and conflicts with core liberal values of pluralism, self-authorship, and cooperation. author: Arezu Fayyazi
title: Domestic Violence and Femicide in Afghanistan: Women Are Denied Protection and Justice
content:
Domestic violence has intensified under Taliban rule since August 2021, as the regime has imposed more than 160 edicts and directives restricting the rights and freedoms of women and girls. By barring women from education and employment, severely limiting their freedom of movement, and denying them meaningful access to justice, the Taliban has deepened women’s dependence on their families and left many with fewer ways to escape abuse or seek protection. In this climate of systemic oppression and impunity, domestic violence can go unchallenged, while women and girls face the devastating risk of femicide.

Reports from The Guardian and Zan Times have recorded 231 cases of femicide across just ten provinces -there are 34 provinces – in Afghanistan since 2021. However, it is important to note that these reports emphasized the fact that these cases of femicide do not represent all of the cases in the country since 2021, given the fact that it’s difficult to record these instances of domestic violence after the Taliban has removed avenues to report these crimes.

The Taliban has dismantled the Ministry of Women’s Affairs, the prosecutor’s office that handled violence against women, and women’s shelters all together. Additionally, women judges and men judges that were trained on domestic violence issues and supported women, have all been removed. With the Taliban’s return to power, roughly 250 female judges lost their jobs and were banned from practicing. All those positions were filled with Taliban members, most of whom have no official training in law. The complete dismantling of all legal protections for women in Afghanistan has contributed to the increased rates of domestic violence in addition to a lack of legal accountability for men who commit domestic violence.

Even worse, the victims of just the recorded cases ranged from 5 to 65. Of these 231 cases, only 58 cases resulted in arrests of the suspect committing violence, only roughly 25% of cases. The lack of accountability for domestic violence is reinforced by the Taliban’s astonishing new Criminal Procedure Regulation of the Courts released in February 2026. In these regulations, it “allows husbands to physically punish their wives as long as the violence does not result in ‘broken bones or serious visible injuries.’” This regulation is evidence of the Taliban’s disregard for the rights, safety, and wellbeing of women. This new regulation just allows domestic violence to occur with no repercussions, and women are left paying the consequences with their dignity and lives. Liza Shams, a victim of domestic violence, passed away after going to the hospital for “being severely beaten” with “multiple fractures to her facial bones.”

The systematic oppression of women has left a huge burden on Afghan women not just physically, but also mentally and emotionally. With the lack of support or possibility to leave a relationship of domestic violence, there has been an increase in suicide due to psychological pressure. According to data from the UN, 7 in 10 women “describe their mental health as ‘bad’ or ‘very bad.’” Hasina, a young woman who was just 22 years old, took her own life after experiencing domestic violence from her husband and his family. Her uncle spoke out and said her death was “a killing caused by violence and oppression, even if the final act was carried out by her own hand.” He goes on to say “at such a young age, she had already gone through so much. She should have been studying, growing and preparing for a brighter future. Instead, she found herself in circumstances where, from her perspective, ending her life appeared to be the only escape.”

There is enough evidence to demonstrate that domestic violence is not just a household issue, but one compounded by a political system that strips women of their autonomy, protections, and opportunities. When women are banned from going to school, earning an income, seeking justice, or becoming independent – escaping an abusive situation is incredibly difficult. The consequences leave women isolated, psychologically distressed, and in the most tragic cases – dead.

Afghan women have repeatedly made clear that they deserve more than expressions of international concern. Their suffering must not remain hidden behind the closed doors of abusive households and be further obscured by the Taliban’s systematic efforts to erase women from public life and silence their voices. Without access to legal protection, education …

author: Valerie Anne
title: ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ Kicked Off Season 23 With a Sapphic Smooch
content:
Grey’s Anatomy came back with a bang. (Well, a smooch. But we’ll get there.) Amelia spent the entire episode getting the cold shoulder from Toni because, as I’m sure you remember, we left them last season with Toni showing up at Amelia’s door to profess her love for her, only to realize a naked Cass was already in Amelia’s apartment.

When we return for season 23(!), Toni is giving Amelia the cold shoulder all day. Amelia desperately wants to talk to her, but Toni isn’t hearing her out. They clash over work decisions, and Amelia starts to get frustrated. And at this point I was afraid the show was ending their storyline. I thought it was going to be a dramatic fight and then back to no wlw relationships on the show. I was thankfully wrong!

Eventually, the day leads Amelia to Toni’s front door, where she apologizes again for sleeping with Cass, and explains it was an emotional reaction to being so sure Toni was about get back together with her ex. She regrets it if it means she would lose Toni. She says she’s truly, madly, deeply in love with Toni and that if Toni is done, she’ll move on, but if not, she really doesn’t want to let what they have died. Toni considers her for a moment but then breaks; she’s still in love with Amelia, and she’s not done. The two kiss about it, and while I doubt their road ahead will be paved with roses and rainbows (especially because Toni’s ex is still in the picture, and goodness knows if/when Cass will return to drop bombs) but I’m glad we at least aren’t done with their story yet. I look forward to seeing what Season 23 will bring for our resident gays; here’s hoping none of them disappear into the parking lot of no return.

author: Admin101
title: Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense
content:
Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN) is excited to announce the publication of

Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense

.


Drawing on organizing experiences of Black Rose/Rosa Negra members across the United States, this pamphlet explores how workers, neighbors, and communities are building collective resistance to ICE and defending their immigrant coworkers, classmates, and loved ones. By connecting struggles across workplaces, schools, and neighborhoods, the

transversal organizing

 approach we prioritize builds solidarity across different sectors of society to confront the interconnected structures of domination that shape our lives.


You can find a downloadable PDF version of the pamphlet at the end of this text.


Two Years of Trump II: Immigrants in the Crosshairs, Resistance Under Attack


Upon returning to office, Donald Trump wasted little time fulfilling his white supremacist campaign pledge of “Mass Deportations Now.” Via a flurry of executive orders and congressional acts his administration reinstated the reviled “family separation” policy; directed virtually unlimited resources to stop a fictitious “invasion” of the country’s borders; and sought to end birthright citizenship. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents blitzed Los Angeles in June 2025 with spectacular raids, followed shortly by similar operations in dozens of cities across the country including New York City; Chicago, IL; New Orleans, LA; and Durham, NC. This “shock and awe” strategy culminated in Operation Metro Surge, a months-long invasion of the Minnesota Twin Cities that deported over 2,000 residents. 


Meanwhile, support for the deportation machine plummeted as collective action against it swelled. Everyday people covered their cars, lawns, and lips with the slogan “Abolish ICE;” as of July 2026, nearly 50% of US adults support such a measure. Both May Days since Trump’s second inauguration centered immigrant defense in their celebrations. Rapid-response networks that keep watch for ICE, document kidnappings, and sometimes disrupt them spread wildly. Know-your-rights training flourished at worksites and community centers. Millions of Red Cards–wallet-sized cards outlining the holder’s constitutional protections around interactions with ICE and other police–were distributed at schools, churches, restaurants, and municipal buildings. Children and their parents caged in concentration camps went on hunger strike as constituents bombarded politicians’ hotlines and town halls demanding humanitarian treatment and release outside their walls.


Popular responses in St. Paul and Minneapolis demonstrate the possibilities of mass resistance. Like the Los Angeles Tenant Union’s community defense centers that countered ICE’s Southern California invasion, organizers reactivated dormant neighborhood networks from the 2020 uprising and began building new ones when word spread that Commander-at-Large Greg Bovino was bringing his paramilitary forces to town. Once Operation Metro Surge launched, everyday Minnesotans refined sophisticated systems to track, delay, and disrupt arrests. ICE agents retaliated by killing rapid-responder Renée Good and shooting Julio C. Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan immigrant targeted for deportation. Instead of cowering from the naked clampdown, neighborhood networks coordinated with unions, churches, and other civil societal organizations to shut down their cities on January 23rd. In its wake, Trump ousted Bovino and immigration enforcement plummeted.


But July 2026 saw record high immigrant detentions since Trump’s return to office with little public opposition. What explains it? ICE’s tactical shifts undoubtedly played a role. Bovino replacement and “Border Czar” Tom Homan traded provocative street operations with quiet detainers at jails and prisons and “targeted operations” at sites protected from activist impediment like airports. Escalating repression has also raised the costs of resistance. ICE’s bevy of brutality has included intimidation, beatings, and shootings, culminating in murdering Good and rapid-responder Alex Pretti. Federal grand juries fish from the shadows for information about our movements, stoking fears of informants that slow our organizing. From the Prairieland defendants to the Minnesota 15 and more, indictments and convictions on flimsy charges could make prosecuting dissidents even easier. Evidentiary discovery in the …

author: Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg
title: Tablets Make Communication Easier Behind Bars – But Deaf People Are Left Behind
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


Tablet computers have revolutionized communication inside prisons for hearing prisoners. Prison systems from across the country — including in

New York

,

California

, and

Illinois

 — have

distributed tens of thousands

 of tablets to incarcerated people, which they can use to call home, watch movies, message loved ones, or attend virtual classes (although they are often

charged predatory fees

 for accessing these benefits). As of 2022,

25 state prison systems

 had tablet distribution programs, according to the Electronic Privacy Information Center. 


But as the rollout of such tablets continues, many deaf incarcerated people have been left behind. 


Disability justice organization HEARD points out that

it’s

unknown

 how many deaf people are incarcerated in U.S. prisons, but a

2015 report

 by the Bureau of Labor Statistics estimated that 6.2 percent of incarcerated people in

state

 and

federal

 prisons have a hearing disability, which would equal about 71,000 people.


Daniel Valenzuela, who is deaf, is incarcerated at Danville Correctional Center in Illinois. Last year, the Illinois Department of Corrections (IDOC)

distributed tablets

 to all incarcerated people. But IDOC blocks videophone capabilities, preventing Valenzuela from communicating in his primary language, American Sign Language (ASL).  


In September, Valenzuela sued the IDOC director for violating the Americans with Disabilities Act.


“I have six kids, four grandkids, and one of my sons is in the military. I cherish and love my family so much,” said Valenzuela in a

press release

 announcing the lawsuit. “I just want to tell them happy birthday and I am so grieved when I can’t call because I don’t want them to think I forgot.”


There are at least three other deaf individuals at Danville who primarily use ASL to communicate, according to the

complaint

 filed by Disability Rights Advocates, Equip for Equality, and the law firm Much Shelist. 


“Across the Illinois Department of Corrections, people can use tablets to communicate with their loved ones, which has been a game changer in removing restrictions on communication,” Valenzuela’s attorney, Rachel Weisberg, the directing attorney at Disability Rights Advocates, told

Truthout

. “But for Mr. Valenzuela and other deaf people who use American Sign Language, that same access simply isn’t available.” 


IDOC did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.


Last year, in addition to distributing tablets to incarcerated people, IDOC

announced

 it would provide every incarcerated person with 775 free domestic phone call minutes per month. In a press release,

IDOC said

 that these initiatives, working in tandem, “enhance family connections and increase access to technology that supports rehabilitation.” 


But deaf prisoners are excluded from accessing these critical programs. 


Unlike hearing prisoners who can use their tablets to make calls from their cells, Valenzuela must get a guard’s permission to walk to another building to use the one videophone that’s available to him. In at least one instance, Valenzuela had to go out in the pouring rain to use the videophone, according to the complaint. 


“When prison officials don’t communicate with deaf/disabled people in ways they can understand, they may be written up for being ‘non-compliant.'”


The videophone is often unavailable because the unit itself breaks down, the prison is on lockdown, or a guard denies his request, according to the complaint. Last year, Valenzuela was unable to speak with his family during the holidays because the phone was not working for 54 straight days, from November 2025 to January 2026. However, if the tablets malfunction, there are several backup phones that incarcerated hearing people can use, the complaint says.


“We’re asking for equal access, as that’s what the law requires,” said Weisberg. “Equal access is not static — it must reflect the benefits currently offered to others and account for the needs of people with disabilities as technology and communication systems evolve.”


These issues are not limited to Illinois. Advocates say incarcerated deaf people have to contend with discriminatory communication practices in prisons throughout the country.


“In prisons where we’ve seen scores of deaf/disabled people, there may only be 2 videophones,” Kah Mendoza, the communications coordinator for

HEARD

, told …

author: APTN National News
title: Manitoba regional chief cleared by investigation, back at work
content:
The

Assembly of First Nations

 says an independent investigation into Manitoba Regional Chief Willie Moore has wrapped up.


According to an email from Andrew Bisson, the organization’s CEO, the investigation “has concluded and, following a review by the AFN Executive, Regional Chief Moore’s temporary leave of absence is complete and he has now returned to the AFN Executive.”


Moore was on a temporary leave since summer for reasons the AFN would not clarify. His reinstatement comes ahead of next week’s

First Nations – First Ministers

 meeting in Ottawa.


It’s not clear what incident Moore was involved with or the nature of the investigation.


Moore,

one of eleven regional chiefs

 at the AFN, currently holds four portfolios on the executive committee, including economic reconciliation and economic development, lands, territories and resources, social development and the management committee.


APTN has reached out to Moore for comment but has not heard back.


He was first elected to the role of regional chief in July 2024.


Prior to that, Moore was a councilor for Nisichawayasihk Cree Nation in northern Manitoba from 2014 to 2022.

AFN investigating ‘incident’ involving Manitoba Regional Chief Willie Moore

author: Anikibawal
title: Lof Juan Currin de Temuco enfrenta una nueva orden de desalojo del único predio en reivindicación que queda de su territorio ancestral.
content:
Durante el mes de junio del año 2026, dos integrantes del Lof Juan Currin fueron denunciados ante el Juzgado de Garantía de Temuco por el empresario Pablo Jacobi Bauman por los delitos de Usurpación u ocupación violenta de inmueble, en el único predio que queda de su territorio ancestral, el cual figura en su Titulo de Merced. Los dos lamgen que se encuentran procesados en la causa son Leonardo Catrileo Chiguaihuan y Oscar Chiguaihuan Chiguaihuan, quien cumple el rol de Lonkopalife en su comunidad. Durante el mes de octubre, el lof y en particular, los lamgen Oscar y Leonardo han sido notificados con una orden de desalojo.


Este no es el primer proceso judicial que interpone el empresario en contra de la comunidad, durante el año 2001, Pablo Jacobi anuncio una querella por destrucción de propiedad privada, ante la negativa del Lof Juan Currin a la instalación de un cerco dentro del terreno que pretendía instalar el empresario para materializar un proyecto inmobiliario en el predio. Durante esos años, Mariquina Trecamán, dirigenta de la comunidad declaro que el empresario Jacobi tendría una visión parcial de la historia del conflicto, ya que este se remonta al año 1950, cuando Alfonso Taito Schneider llegó al lugar como arrendatario, donde instaló una fábrica de ladrillos, en palabras de Mariquina Trecamán «Este señor fue designado como tutor de un menor de la comunidad, quien al fallecer ambos padres quedó al desamparo. Valiéndose de esta situación, no sólo se apoderó del terreno del menor, sino que se apropió de casi todo el terreno de la comunidad Juan Currín utilizando distintas maniobras en tribunales» (fuente: https://mapuche.info/archivo/news02/austral010528.html).


El Lof Juan Currin lleva décadas resistiendo en este predio ante la usurpación y despojo de casi la totalidad de su territorio ancestral, arrinconados entre edificios y proyectos inmobiliarios han logrado mantener y preservar sus practiiicas sociales, políticas, culturales y espirituales, espacios ceremoniales como un un Rewe y Paliwe, ademas en el lugar se emplazan viviendas pertenecientes a las familias de la comunidad.


 A continuación, compartimos una declaración del lamgen Oscar Chiguaihuan Chiguaihuan, Lonkopalife de la comunidad:


«Bueno, yo soy Óscar Chiguaihuan. Hace tiempo atrás recibí una denuncia aquí en mi territorio, pertenezco a la comunidad Juan Currín. Hubo una denuncia hace tiempo atrás por usurpación violenta, según yo… le usurpé el territorio a Pablo Jacobi, me acusa de haber puesto un rewe, el rewe era de mi abuela y tiene más de 30 años,… me imagino yo que tiene, yo tengo 35 años… yo me crié ahí, siempre había un rewe ahí y el winka me echa la culpa a mí que yo puse un rewe. No es lógico lo que dice.

Esta comunidad es muy antigua, tengo documentos donde se registra la comunidad, el lof, el título de Merced tiene muchos años, documentos de 1922 hacia estos años, hay documentos de que la comunidad está asentada aquí en este territorio y sin embargo hoy día me acusan a mí de yo usurpar territorio donde yo he sido toda la vida de aquí.


Y pasa que después de la denuncia, hoy día llega otra mala noticia, de que el Winka y sus abogados pidieron una audiencia de urgencia en Fiscalía, no sé cómo se harán esos temas y llegaron un acuerdo de desalojar aquí a la comunidad, digamos, despojarnos de donde tenemos el Rewe, que es un lugar ancestral para nosotros lo tomamos como donde hacemos nuestras ceremonias, jugamos al palín, tenemos nuestra salida hacia digamos hacia la hacia la calle, mi familia circula por aquí todos los días y nos quieren encerrar prácticamente, nos aislarían, no tendríamos salida, nada. No entiendo lo que quieren hacer los Winka, pero nosotros queremos evitarlo realmente porque no sería lógico que nos dejen encerrados, sin salida, ni siquiera caminando.


Entonces pasa que salió la audiencia que pueden desalojarnos y nosotros estamos en contra y queremos apoyo, necesitamos que la gente haga visible todavía como el winka usurpa la tierra, se empeñan en despojarnos de nuestra forma de ser, se niegan a reconocer los que nosotros todavía hacemos, nuestro guillatü, nuestro palines, hacemos ceremonia, celebramos Wetripantü, entonces nos van a despojar de todo eso si logran su acometido los winka. Nosotros como comunidad, digamos, como familia siempre hemos sido afectados, siempre hemos tenido que estar luchando. Yo tengo 35 años, pero hay registro de lucha de mi comunidad mucho más de la edad que tengo yo, hay mucha …

author: CMI Argentina
title: Súper El Niño: la barbarie capitalista recalienta el planeta y amenaza con multiplicar el hambre
content:
El calentamiento global agrava los riesgos de un fenómeno climático extremo. UNICEF advierte que 25,8 millones de niños de América Latina y el Caribe están expuestos a sequías e inundaciones. Detrás de la emergencia climática, una economía organizada para garantizar las ganancias y no las necesidades humanas.


Por Adrián Flores para Red Eco Alternativo


El mundo se encamina hacia un episodio de El Niño potencialmente histórico. El 10 de septiembre, la Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica de Estados Unidos (NOAA) estimó en más del 90% la probabilidad de un fenómeno muy fuerte durante el otoño y el invierno boreales de 2026-2027. Sus efectos podrían extender las sequías, las inundaciones y las pérdidas agrícolas en distintas regiones del planeta. 

Fuente:

NOAA


El problema no es solamente climático: es profundamente social. El calentamiento global, provocado principalmente por las emisiones derivadas de la actividad humana, agrava los riesgos sobre los que actúa El Niño. Pero sus consecuencias no golpean a todos por igual. Mientras los grandes capitales cuentan con recursos para proteger sus negocios, millones de trabajadores, campesinos y comunidades vulnerables quedan expuestos a la pérdida de sus viviendas, sus cosechas y sus fuentes de ingresos.


Las cifras son alarmantes. Según UNICEF, 25,8 millones de niños de América Latina y el Caribe —uno de cada siete— viven en zonas expuestas a sequías e inundaciones asociadas con El Niño. El organismo advirtió sobre los riesgos para la alimentación, el acceso al agua potable, la salud y la educación. Además, de los 53,8 millones de dólares solicitados para prepararse y responder a emergencias en la región durante 2026, el 55% seguía sin financiación al cierre de junio. 

Fuente:

UNICEF,

 28 de septiembre de 2026. 


La amenaza se extiende al hambre mundial. El Programa Mundial de Alimentos estima que El Niño podría empujar a otros 49 millones de personas hacia la inseguridad alimentaria aguda, elevando de 225 a 274 millones el total de personas afectadas en los países analizados. La pérdida de cosechas, el encarecimiento de los alimentos y los elevados costos de producción pueden convertir una alteración climática en una catástrofe alimentaria.

Fuente:

PMA


Pero el hambre no es una consecuencia inevitable de la naturaleza. Es también el resultado de un sistema que convierte los alimentos en mercancías, subordina la producción a la rentabilidad y condena a millones de personas a no poder comprar aquello que necesitan para vivir. El capitalismo destruye ecosistemas, impulsa la explotación intensiva de los recursos naturales y traslada sus costos a las mayorías populares.


Frente a esta barbarie, no alcanza con declaraciones ambientales ni con medidas de emergencia insuficientes. Se necesitan inversiones públicas, prevención, protección de los pequeños productores y garantías de acceso al agua, la vivienda y la alimentación. Eso exige enfrentar los intereses económicos que subordinan la vida a la ganancia.


El súper El Niño expone una contradicción central de nuestra época: la humanidad posee los conocimientos y la capacidad productiva para garantizar una vida digna, pero el capitalismo convierte esa posibilidad en privilegio. La lucha contra la catástrofe climática es inseparable de la lucha de clases y de la reorganización socialista de la economía al servicio de las necesidades humanas.


Fuente:

https://redeco.com.ar/nacional/ambiente/78021-super-el-nino-la-barbarie-capitalista-recalienta-el-planeta-y-amenaza-con-multiplicar-el-hambre


La entrada

Súper El Niño: la barbarie capitalista recalienta el planeta y amenaza con multiplicar el hambre

 se publicó primero en

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))

.

author: Maria Martha Bruno
title: ‘Leilão às avessas’: vitória de Flávio consolidaria interferência dos EUA no Brasil
content:
A duas semanas do segundo turno das eleições brasileiras, o norte-americano Robert Kennedy Jr., secretário de Saúde dos Estados Unidos e expoente do movimento antivacina, esteve no Rio de Janeiro para casar seu filho, Conor Kennedy. A noiva era a cantora Giulia Be, que, apesar de ter declarado voto em Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva em 2022, é membro de outro clã da direita, a família Marinho, ligada aos Bolsonaro. Seu pai, Paulo Marinho, foi um dos principais nomes da campanha de Jair em 2018 e é suplente de Flávio no Senado. 


A cerimônia religiosa foi na Igreja Nossa Senhora do Carmo da Antiga Sé, no centro do Rio de Janeiro, onde Dom Pedro I e Dom Pedro II foram coroados. Com pompa e circunstância, a celebração ganhou cobertura internacional. 


Apenas uma semana depois do casamento, em São Paulo, apoiadores de Flávio Bolsonaro carregaram um míssil inflável com os dizeres “Trump nuke Brazil” (Trump, faça um ataque nuclear ao Brasil), em mais uma demonstração de subserviência ao governo de Donald Trump.


Casamento de direita reúne André Marinho (ao centro) e Robert Kennedy Jr. (à esquerda) no Rio de Janeiro, duas semanas antes das eleições


Os dois eventos revelam a crescente proximidade da extrema direita brasileira com a norte-americana. Uma eventual vitória de Flávio representaria a consolidação do projeto por trás da Doutrina Donroe, que promove o retorno do domínio norte-americano sobre a América Latina, na opinião do cientista político

Guilherme Casarões

, da Florida International University.


“A Doutrina Monroe, a original do século 19, tinha como ideia básica proteger o hemisfério americano dos interesses europeus e consolidar a hegemonia dos EUA. O que o Trump tenta fazer agora é justamente revitalizá-la com características novas, que se baseiam não só na imposição de um certo poderio militar e de relações econômicas, mas também envolvem a construção de uma aliança ideológica nas Américas”.


Terras raras: do fundo do poço para o bolso de Trump Jr.


No início de abril, André Marinho, o irmão da noiva do casamento no Rio, esteve nos EUA, onde se encontrou com o vice-presidente americano, J.D. Vance. O encontro foi articulado por Robert Kennedy Jr.. Na ocasião, Marinho disse ter tratado com Vance da expansão do crime organizado no Rio de Janeiro e das conexões de facções criminosas com redes internacionais.


De lá pra cá, uma profusão de digitais dos EUA apareceu nas articulações do bolsonarismo para as eleições de 2026, da abertura de uma filial brasileira da

Rockbridge

, rede de financiadores da extrema direita criada por Vence, ao

financiamento

 do filme “Dark Horse”, realizado por meio de um fundo estabelecido no Texas.


Na frente econômica, chamou atenção o documento produzido por André Marinho com as possíveis vantagens de uma administração de Flávio Bolsonaro para o governo e os negócios da família Trump. O “Prosperity Partnership”, de autoria do irmão da noiva, mostra como os EUA explorariam terras raras – elementos químicos essenciais para a produção de ímãs de alta potência em turbinas, eletrônicos e armamento – em mais um governo de extrema direita no Brasil.


Revelado

 pelo jornalista Guilherme Amado, o plano foi elaborado em março deste ano, cerca de duas semanas antes de Marinho viajar aos EUA para se reunir com Vance. Marinho negou que o documento, com a capa “Flávio Bolsonaro | 2026 Campaign”, tivesse relação com a campanha bolsonarista.


Segundo o “Prosperity Partnership”, um novo governo Bolsonaro “posicionará o Brasil como o principal fornecedor e polo de processamento de minerais críticos alinhado ao Ocidente no Hemisfério Ocidental”; não tornará o país “dependente” de cadeias de processamento chinesas; e, por fim, “se alinhará com os Estados Unidos na construção de um sistema de abastecimento paralelo”. O documento também fala em “aceleração no processo regulatório”, em consonância com o

programa de governo

 de Flávio Bolsonaro, que, ao tratar do tema, promete “licenciamento ágil e técnico”.


Procurado pela reportagem, Marinho afirmou que o “assunto é superado exatamente por não haver qualquer consequência prática na realidade”. Em seguida, mandou nota em que disse que “o estudo foi elaborado por iniciativa exclusivamente pessoal, como um exercício hipotético de análise de cenários. Não se tratava de proposta oficial nem foi produzida a pedido de qualquer campanha, autoridade ou organização.”

author: anred
title: «Que no se apague la salud»: residentes y concurrentes realizan «Marcha de las Velas» contra el ajuste en los hospitales porteños
content:
Foto: archivo La Izquierda Diario


Bajo la consigna “La salud pública se defiende”, la Asamblea de Residentes y Concurrentes de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires (que nuclea a residentes y concurrentes de hospitales y centros de salud porteños) convocó para hoy, jueves 22 de octubre, a una nueva «Marcha de las Velas» en defensa de la salud pública, que partirá a las 18.30 desde el cruce de avenida Las Heras y Bulnes, en el Parque Las Heras, y finalizará a las 20 en Plaza Houssay. La convocatoria se realiza en el marco de la quinta semana de un plan de lucha por la recomposición salarial y contra el deterioro de las condiciones laborales. La Asamblea denuncia una pérdida del poder adquisitivo de 30 puntos desde 2023, jornadas laborales extensas, dificultades crecientes para sostener la atención sanitaria, y amenazas y hostigamientos contra quienes participan de las medidas de fuerza, que incluyen pedidos de listados de trabajadores adherentes y registros de asistencia que, según denunciaron, consignaron la palabra “Paro” incluso para residentes que estaban cubriendo guardias.

Por ANRed.


La

Asamblea de Residentes y Concurrentes de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires

 convocó para

este jueves 22 de octubre a una nueva movilización en defensa de la salud pública

. La «

Marcha de las Velas

» partirá a las

18.30 desde avenida Las Heras y Bulnes, en el Parque Las Heras, y finalizará a las 20 en Plaza Houssay

. La jornada se inscribe en la quinta semana de un plan de lucha por la recomposición salarial y contra el deterioro de las condiciones laborales.


El conflicto comenzó a mediados de septiembre. Desde entonces, se realizaron paros y movilizaciones semanales con participación de hospitales y centros de salud de la Ciudad. El 1 de octubre, residentes y concurrentes volvieron a parar durante 24 horas y marcharon hasta el Ministerio de Salud porteño, a cargo de

Fernán González Bernaldo de Quirós

. En una jornada anterior, el paro había contado con la adhesión de 25 hospitales y efectores, según el relevamiento difundido por organizaciones del sector.


El reclamo central es una

recomposición salarial del 30% para recuperar poder adquisitivo

, junto con

adicionales por guardias y por especialidades críticas

, y

un bono compensatorio retroactivo

. La Asamblea denuncia que los ingresos quedaron rezagados frente a la inflación.


Imagen: La Izquierda Diario


Las condiciones de trabajo también forman parte del conflicto:

las y los residentes denuncian que pueden llegar a trabajar entre 70 y 90 horas semanales, con guardias de 24 horas e, incluso, extensiones de 36 horas.


Los concurrentes, por su parte, denuncian que realizan tareas sin percibir salario y sin contar con derechos laborales básicos como cobertura por accidentes de trabajo.

 La Asamblea plantea que estas condiciones afectan tanto a quienes sostienen las guardias y los servicios como a la calidad de la atención que recibe la población.


En la misma línea, a los reclamos salariales y por coindiciones laborales se suman las

denuncias de hostigamiento y persecución por parte de las autoridades sanitarias porteñas

. Desde la Asamblea señalaron que en las últimas semanas

recibieron avisos informales sobre posibles descuentos

, pedidos de

 listados con nombre y apellido de quienes participaron de las medidas de fuerza

 y

registros de asistencia en los que figuraba “Paro” incluso para residentes que se encontraban cubriendo guardias

.


Foto: Maximiliano Luna / Télam.


La Asamblea también advierte sobre el

vaciamiento del conjunto de la salud pública, las dificultades para acceder a medicamentos y turnos y la emergencia en salud mental

. También rechaza

cualquier intento de fragmentar la carrera profesional regulada por la Ley 6.035 y plantea la necesidad de ampliar la organización colectiva a los trabajadores de planta

. En ese sentido, la propuesta de realizar asambleas hospitalarias conjuntas apunta a reunir demandas que atraviesan a distintos sectores del sistema sanitario.


Imagen: Bernardino Avila.


Antes de la Marcha de las Velas,

una funcionaria del Comité de Docencia e Investigación (CODEI) recibirá a representantes del sector en una instancia de diálogo, según informó Prensa Obrera

. La Asamblea anticipó que llevará allí el reclamo de recomposición salarial y la necesidad de respuestas concretas. Mientras tanto, sostiene la convocatoria a la movilización y reclama que el Ministerio de Salud escuche sus demandas sin represalias contra …

author: Darío Aranda
title: Miguel Mirra: "Cuando la comunidad participa en contar su historia, la recupera para la lucha"
content:
Por Ivana Carino


Desde mediados de la década del 80 Miguel Mirra trabaja una filmografía que recupera lo que suele quedar por fuera del plano de las narrativas industriales: las luchas de los pueblos originarios, los conflictos territoriales y las resistencias socioambientales, entre otros temas. Director de cine, guionista y docente, se formó en historia y antropología antes de pasar por la escuela de cine de Avellaneda.


Nacido en Lanús en 1950, en el seno de una familia de clase trabajadora, Mirra relata su recorrido con calidez, humor y un particular gusto por las anécdotas. Entiende

la cámara como una herramienta de lucha

: no solo para registrar y visibilizar los conflictos, sino también para

construir memoria, poner en circulación experiencias y hacer cine junto a quienes protagonizan esas historias

. Desde

La máscara de la conquista

 (1985)

, hasta sus trabajos más recientes, hay una preocupación que atraviesa su recorrido: que el documental acompañe las resistencias y permita que quienes las protagonizan se reconozcan también en las imágenes.


Foto: Télam


Entre el documental y la ficción


“Llegué al documental porque no sabía hacer otra cosa”, bromea Mirra. En la escuela de cine de Avellaneda había dos vertientes, documental y ficción, y él probó las dos. Su primera realización con equipo completo fue una ficción de época ambientada en la mal llamada "Conquista de América",

La máscara de la conquista

, rodada en 16 milímetros en 1985, con escenas filmadas en Mar del Plata y Córdoba. “Para una escuela era un lujo”, recuerda.


Fue durante ese rodaje cuando comenzó a explorar el cruce entre ambos lenguajes. Había escenas que no sabía cómo resolver y decidió filmarlas como documental: “Les planteé a los actores que siguieran más o menos el guion y las filmamos en el aquí y ahora, donde había sucedido aquello”. El resultado funcionó mejor de lo que esperaba. “Me di cuenta que había quedado bueno”, recuerda. Allí comenzó a descubrir las posibilidades del documental.


Ese descubrimiento tomó forma con

Hombres de barro

, rodada entre 1986 y 1987, y estrenada en 1988. Mirra la define como “el puntapié” de sus trabajos como documentalista. Fue, dice, una experiencia extraordinaria. El equipo, de cinco personas, filmaba en las Sierras de Zenta, en el límite entre Jujuy y Salta, cuando se cruzó con una camioneta en la que uno de sus ocupantes llevaba una cámara. “Nos preguntamos ¿quiénes son estos?”, recuerda. Era Miguel Pereira, que estaba filmando

La deuda interna

 (1988).


A partir de entonces, Mirra fue y vino entre el documental y la ficción. En

Crónica de un extraño

 (1998)

 retomó la historia de Eulogio Frites, abogado kolla y referente del derecho indígena en América, a quien había entrevistado para

Hombres de barro

. Frites le había contado que su familia lo había entregado a la familia administradora de un ingenio, donde pudo estudiar y recibirse de abogado. A partir de esa historia, Mirra construyó un relato de ficción sobre un padre que viaja a Buenos Aires en busca de su hijo, un joven que se había alejado de su comunidad para probar suerte como boxeador. “Hay parte del documental anterior y otras son ficción”, explica.


Pero no todas las historias admiten ese cruce. En sus documentales biográficos sobre Adolfo Pérez Esquivel,

Otro mundo es posible

 (2010);

Darío Santillán,


la dignidad rebelde

 (2012); y

Norita, Nora Cortiñas

 (2013), la ficción no tuvo lugar. En el caso de Santillán, es categórico: “Ahí no correspondía meter ficción. Trabajamos con la gente que lo conoció”.


La exploración de esas formas híbridas continuó con

Fuego en Casabindo

 (2022). Mirra llegó a la historia a partir del descubrimiento de una ópera sobre la rebelión kolla de 1874 en la puna jujeña, cuando unos 2.000 kollas se enfrentaron primero al ejército provincial y luego al nacional, en la

Batalla de Quera

. La investigación lo llevó a escribir un guion que pone en diálogo la ópera con los acontecimientos históricos y construye un personaje ficcional que funciona como nexo entre ambos planos.


La película debía exhibirse en Casabindo, pero antes fue presentada en San Salvador de Jujuy. Mirra recuerda que, cuando estaba por entrar a la sala, vio llegar una columna de personas: eran kollas que iban a verla. Al finalizar la proyección le regalaron un pequeño toro de porcelana. “Es uno de los recuerdos más lindos que tengo de ese momento”, cuenta.
